What I wanted to do in beginning the analysis of this justiciable interest question is call to the court's attention. The fact that this is not a novel question in interpreting the tolling statute, while the justiciable interest issue in particular has not arisen. There is a long history of Texas courts dealing with the question of how to deal with dismissals that are prudential or discretionary and a failure to exercise jurisdiction. And the court doesn't need to make new law here. You simply need to follow existing precedent on this issue precedent that the appellants don't want to deal with in their briefs, Mr. Townsend doesn't allude to here in his argument because it forecloses the argument. I think the important rule comes from the McDonald's treatise from 1984. This was the accepted interpretation of this statute in 1984 that the tolling statute includes dismissals based on an impropriety of exercising jurisdiction in a particular matter. The legislature knew that that was the understanding of this statute. When it codified the statute in 1985, the legislature could have altered that interpretation and did not. It's acquiesced in that interpretation that goes back generations. Now, I think that the appellant's reply brief actually gives us some valuable context, because as we explained in our brief, this issue comes up most frequently in the problem of supplemental or pendant jurisdiction, where a federal district court has federal question jurisdiction and has supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims. If it dismisses the federal claims, it has discretion then to maintain jurisdiction over the state law claims or to dismiss them. If it dismisses the state law claim, which is a matter of judicial discretion, it had original jurisdiction over those claims. It has been held for generations in Texas that the tolling statute applies under that rule, that the statute reaches the impropriety of exercising jurisdiction. But what the reply brief illustrates that I think amplifies that rule is that rule didn't even originate in the context of supplemental or pendant jurisdiction as it was once known. It originated with the doctrine of abstention, because the original case in this line of authority is the Burford versus Sun Oil decision, which is one of the landmark cases from the United States Supreme Court over the abstention doctrine. And in that case, the U.S. Supreme Court said federal courts ought not exercise jurisdiction they had. They ought to defer to the state courts to exercise jurisdiction in the first instance. And so when the case went back and was filed anew in state court, the Austin court in the Burford case said that situation triggered tolling. And so from the very first days of this statute, within a decade after the statute was enacted, the courts interpreted the tolling statute to reach a discretionary determination by a court of proper jurisdiction not to exercise that jurisdiction. There's a third example. And I apologize to the court that we didn't explain it in the briefs, but it came to my attention as we were preparing for the argument. The Chief Justice Raddick, it's an opinion that you dealt with a few years ago. It's Janender versus Kirkwood. And the citation of that case is 506 Southwest 3rd 508. And in that case, this court dealt with the question about what to do with a voluntary dismissal. And the court said correctly, I think that voluntarily dismissing a claim doesn't trigger the tolling statute. But you distinguish that from a federal case in which a federal district court had declined to exercise jurisdiction based on the forum nonconvenience doctrine. And you held that was an appropriate exercise of the statute. It just didn't apply. So you have three examples that the Texas courts have recognized of situations where courts declined to exercise jurisdiction that they technically have, and the courts have held that as a proper occasion to invoke the tolling statute. Now, unless the appellants can make some sense of their rule with that line of authority, they're asking you to diverge from a body of law that has been settled since at least 1944. And they're asking you to do so in a way that will have dramatic consequences for future cases. Because if their position is held to be correct, then all of those cases, particularly the supplemental jurisdiction cases, which come up with some frequency, where a federal district court declines to exercise its jurisdiction, will leave plaintiffs with time-barred claims despite the fact they filed timely claims in federal court and properly invoked the original jurisdiction of the federal court, yet they would be time-barred. The appellants have given you no way to reconcile their position with that consequence. In fact, as I read the reply brief, they criticized these cases for being wrongly reasoned. They would celebrate that outcome. I don't think the court can take that approach. I think that in the Texas Supreme Court's decisions in dealing with this justiciable interest issue, it recognizes you have to think about what are the consequences of a ruling. In re USAA says in dealing with the question of jurisdiction, we look at the consequences. The legislature intends a just and reasonable result of its statutes. The likelihood that it intended to close the door on litigants in Texas after generations of precedent is, I submit, unlikely.

speaker: russellpost
text: Your Honor, I think there's two dimensions to the question. The first is, what is the significance of the evolution in the Supreme Court's understanding of jurisdiction over the last generation? The second is, what is the particular meaning of that language, lack of jurisdiction in the statute? Because, remember, we're construing a statute here. We're not looking for the platonic ideal of the idea of jurisdiction. We're asking, what did the legislature mean when it used the term jurisdiction, when it codified the statute in 1985? At that time, jurisdiction had an accepted meaning consistent with these cases that I'm alluding to, consistent with the McDonald's Treatise, and consistent with the understood interpretation of the word jurisdiction at that time as being a comprehensive term that has many different meanings. I think what's most important, because it goes specifically to the question before the court, the phrase lack of jurisdiction, as used in this statute, is a term of art that was recognized by Black's Law Dictionary at the generation in which this statute was enacted to include both a lack of subject matter jurisdiction, as Mr. Townsend argues, and also a circumstance in which conditions essential to the exercise of the court's jurisdiction have not been complied with. That's exactly what you have when a party who attempts to intervene is stricken for lack of a justiciable interest. And so I think this situation falls squarely within that contemporaneous understanding. The Supreme Court's development of the doctrine of jurisdiction over the last generation favors the appellees in this situation, because it underscores, and the Supreme Court has been very forthright in recognizing it, that in the past century, the word jurisdiction was used very broadly to include not only restrictions on the subject matter jurisdiction of the court, such as the statutory limit that Mr. Townsend alluded to in his argument, but also a variety of considerations that affect a party's ability to secure relief on the merits. Now, the court has since taught us, ever since Duvai versus Causey in 2000, the court has signaled, we're going to retreat from that understanding of definition. We want the definition of jurisdiction to be a true jurisdictional concept to minimize collateral attacks on judgments. But in so doing, the court made it explicit that that was a repudiation of the prior century of jurisprudence, and it was that prior century of jurisprudence that the legislature knew when it enacted the statute. And so whatever jurisdiction means for purposes of the court's constitutional jurisdiction today, that's separate from the question of what this statute means when it alludes to a lack of jurisdiction. And on that issue, I think the precedent and the contemporary understanding of this statute are all in one accord. A lack of jurisprudence falls squarely within the heart of that traditional understanding of the statute. And so we would ask that the court approve.
